prompt: Match each role to the question it asks.

pairs.right: Why are we building this, and what comes first?
How will a person use it?

right_distractors: Which function should hold this code?

prompt: Marta wants online balances for gift cards. Who decides whether that is worth two sprints?

choices.why: She supplies the cost; priority is product's call.
Testing informs risk, not priority.
Right. She decides; the team makes the cost honest.
Order of speaking decides nothing.

prompt: What is the happy path in a design?

choices.why: Right. The other cases are where questions help.

choices.text: The quickest route through the code
choices.why: It is about the person using it, not the code.

choices.text: The design the customer likes best
choices.why: It is a case, not a preference.
Review is unrelated.

prompt: When does Diego's way of thinking help most?
hint: Before or after the assumption is built?

choices.text: Only on the last day, before release
choices.why: That is where the negative balance was found, late.
Then it is the most expensive rung of the ladder.
Checks cover what a script sees.
Right. Refunds and negative balances are cheap to catch there.

prompt: Match each surprise at #38's review to who raised it.
hint: Each role saw a different kind of problem.

pairs.left: Gift cards are for the shop only
The balance has its own screen
The balance can go below zero

prompt: Every fact behind #38's surprises existed at the start of the sprint. Why did they appear at the end?

choices.why: Speed would only have brought the same review sooner.

choices.text: The work passed along like a relay
choices.why: Right. What each handover lost surfaced at the end.

choices.text: The sprint was too short to fit it all
choices.why: A longer one would have pushed the surprises later.
Diego did, which is how one surprise was found.

prompt: Why does a relay feel efficient and still cost more?
hint: What gets lost at each handover?

choices.why: Right. And they arrive looking like someone's fault.
Headcount is the same in both shapes.
The cost is what is lost, not the meeting.
QA is the last runner, not skipped.

prompt: Which earlier lesson made the same argument as this one?

choices.why: That was about readers of the history.
That was about storage.

choices.text: Lesson 17, on the ladder of done
choices.why: Right. The lower a problem is caught, the less it costs.
That was about sharing commits.

prompt: Paulo's drawing shows the gift card page when everything works. Which states are worth asking him about? Choose all that apply.
hint: The cases the drawing does not show.

choices.why: Yes. What does the page say?
Yes. A real case on the second visit.

choices.text: The name is forty characters long
choices.why: Yes. Layouts break on long text.
That one he has already drawn.

prompt: On the second day of #38, what would have brought Marta's surprise forward?

choices.why: The review would still be the first look.
Right. Shop only? would have come on day two.
Tests check the code, not the intent.
That is when it happened.

prompt: Why write I've assumed gift cards work online too in the pull request?
hint: An assumption in your head cannot be corrected.

choices.why: It is for correction, not defence.
Nothing requires it; it is a habit.
Right. Marta would have answered at once.
Length is not the point.

prompt: Why does a pull request tell QA how to try the change?

choices.why: It points at the risk; exploring still happens.

choices.text: QA tests where the risk is
choices.why: Right. Better than guessing.
Review and testing are different steps.
Many can; the note saves time either way.

prompt: Marta asks for online balances. Which reply helps her most?

choices.why: A refusal gives her nothing to decide with.

choices.text: Two sprints; shop-only is three days.
choices.why: Right. A cost and an alternative; she decides.

choices.text: Sure, I'll start on it tonight, no problem.
choices.why: Agreeing without a cost hides the trade-off.
The cost is the developer's to give.

prompt: Why ask Marta how anybody will know #38 worked?
hint: If something must be dropped, what stays?

choices.text: To set a deadline for the work
choices.why: The answer is a result, not a date.

choices.text: To test how well she knows the product
choices.why: It is a real question, not a quiz.
It is a habit, not a rule.
Right. Fewer calls to the shop, for instance.

prompt: Put these habits in the order they happen in a ticket's life.
hint: Before building, while building, when handing over.
items: Read the ticket with product, design and QA
Tell QA what changed and how to try it
trap: Asking only at handover brings the questions back to the end.

prompt: Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two are about what the roles are not.

choices.text: QA is only the last gate before release
choices.why: QA helps most before the code exists.
Yes. It decides how the page works, and what it says when things go wrong.

choices.text: Product decides how the code is built
choices.why: Product decides what and why.
Yes. The argument of the whole lesson.
